money_at_stake.rationale: Revised DOWN from GT_100B after an adversarial fetch check found the sole evidence item behind that band did not say what this appraisal attributed to it. The eunews.it article states 2025 EU total energy-product imports (oil, LNG, gaseous gas and coal combined) at 336.7 billion euros, down from 693.4 billion euros four years earlier; it contains no 404bn pipeline / 281bn LNG / 685bn combined gas-specific figures. Search corroboration points to those specific pipeline and LNG totals living on IEEFA's EU Gas Flows Tracker and European LNG Tracker, but both pages returned HTTP 403 to every fetch this session and the Wayback Machine could not be retrieved through this session's tools either (a categorical block, not a missing-snapshot result), so per the venue rule the figures are dropped rather than kept on a search engine's secondhand paraphrase alone. What survives direct fetch: Eurostat's own Statistics Explained page states EU LNG imports ran at a monthly average value of 4.5 billion euros in 2025, a gas-specific run rate of roughly 54 billion euros a year on its own. Separately, Global Energy Monitor's Europe Gas Tracker prices the committed LNG-terminal and pipeline buildout closing Europe's import-capacity gap at 84.1 billion euros (44.4bn for LNG terminals, 39.7bn for pipelines) -- a one-time capex figure, not an annual rate. Pipeline gas is the larger half of EU gas imports by volume (55 percent versus LNG's 45 percent, per Eurostat) and ran at a monthly average value of 17.0 billion euros in the 2022 crisis year (roughly 200 billion euros annualized), but no fetchable primary source this session gave a 2025-specific euro total for pipeline gas alone, only percentage changes (import value +3.4% year on year, volume -5.3%, per Eurostat). That gap is not papered over with an invented combined total. On the figures actually confirmed by direct fetch (LNG's ~54bn-euro/yr run rate and the 84.1bn-euro committed buildout), the pool clears 10 billion dollars comfortably, but nothing fetchable this session ties EU gas spending specifically, in the current year, to a number north of 100 billion dollars, so B10_100 rather than GT_100B is the band the evidence actually supports. Goldman Sachs, quoted via OilPrice.com, puts December 2026 TTF potentially needing to clear 100 euros per megawatt-hour in a slow Middle-East-LNG-recovery scenario, which is upside price risk sitting on top of this baseline, not counted into the band itself. Re-verified 2026-08-30 18:00Z: every evidence item below was independently fetched this pass and every figure it quotes was found verbatim on the page. No item was dropped and the band is unchanged.

public_reach.rationale: Genuinely split down the middle rather than dominated either way, so scored at the boundary between the mixed anchor and the large-unlisted-share anchor rather than rounded toward the story. LNG is 45 percent of EU gas imports and pipeline gas the other 55 percent. Within LNG, the United States supplied 57.9 percent in 2025, and US LNG export capacity is dominated by listed operators, Cheniere, Venture Global and Sempra's Cameron terminal chief among them, which is real reach. But Russia remained the EU's second largest LNG source at 13.5 percent, sanctioned and unreachable, and Qatar's wholly state-owned QatarEnergy holds a meaningful share of the remainder. Within pipeline gas, Norway supplied 54.4 percent, mostly through the listed Equinor and its listed partners Shell and TotalEnergies, which is reach, but Algeria's state-owned Sonatrach and Azerbaijan's state-owned SOCAR together carry roughly a quarter of pipeline volume and neither is investable. Blending the two halves by their supplier shares puts a bit over half the money's origin with listed or listed-adjacent operators and leaves a genuinely large remainder with state entities and one sanctioned supplier, which is the split anchor rather than the clearly-reachable one. Repair note: the second evidence item previously cited PGJ Online for the Norway 54.4 percent figure and attributed it to Eurostat. A direct fetch found that article covers only a 2.3 percent year-on-year volume decline in Norwegian pipeline exports and states neither a 54.4 percent share nor Eurostat as its source. The 54.4 percent figure is real: it is stated directly on Eurostat's own Statistics Explained page and independently in the Rigzone article already cited below for the LNG breakdown, which also gives the pipeline breakdown (Norway 54.4%, North Africa 18.7%, Russia 11.6%, UK 8.12%, Azerbaijan 7.19%). The citation has been corrected to the article that actually states the claim. The original also carried an uncited 'roughly 8 percent' for Qatar's LNG share; this session's own direct fetch of the already-cited Rigzone article confirms Qatar at 11 Bcm, 8.08 percent of 2025 EU LNG imports, matching the original estimate almost exactly, so the figure is restored here in the rationale (not added as a separately scored claim, since it does not move the reach split already found: Qatar is state-owned QatarEnergy either way).

capture_odds.rationale: Two structural facts pull in opposite directions and the evidence for the negative one is the more concrete of the two. For capture: Norway's near-majority position on non-Russian pipeline gas and Europe's limited regasification slots are the kind of scarce, qualification-gated capacity that normally holds price, and Equinor, Shell, TotalEnergies and ConocoPhillips are putting fresh capital behind it, sanctioning the Troll TWIN subsea project specifically to grow European supply. Against capture: the exact kind of profit spike this occurrence would generate is already the stated target of policy. Finance ministers from five EU states (Germany, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Austria) publicly called for a bloc-wide windfall tax on energy companies in April 2026, citing the same price surge. Separately, Transport & Environment's August 2026 analysis put EU-attributable excess profit at roughly 7.5 billion euros across eight large oil companies (Shell, BP, TotalEnergies, Eni, Orlen, Repsol, OMV, Moeve) in the first half of 2026 (1.6bn in Q1, 5.9bn in Q2), precisely the kind of number a windfall tax is levied against. Separately again, most of the reachable infrastructure layer, the regasification terminals owned by listed utilities such as National Grid and Enagas, earns a regulated tariff return that is capped independent of how high the spot gas price goes, so the specific price spike this occurrence produces mostly bypasses the part of the chain that is easiest to reach and lands on the merchant supply layer that is under live windfall-tax pressure. Repair note: the original evidence cited a single CNBC article for both the ministers' letter and the 7.5 billion euro profit figure, with a 'tracking group' attribution. A direct fetch of that CNBC URL was blocked (403); a fetchable Euronews report of the same April 4 letter confirms the ministers' call but contains no profit figure at all, and the CNBC piece plausibly never carried one either. The 7.5 billion euro figure is real but belongs to a separate, later, dated source: Transport & Environment's own August 2026 analysis, now cited directly below rather than folded into the April story.

timing_fit.rationale: The squeeze is not a one-winter blip: it is live now and the supply response committed against it runs into the back half of this repo's window. Storage sits at an 18-year seasonal low heading into the 2026-2027 heating season right now (EU storage was only 57.1% full at the start of August 2026, the lowest for that date in records back to 2009), which is inside the window by definition, and the structural fix, new non-Russian pipeline and LNG capacity, lands in stages through 2028 to 2030 rather than all at once: the Troll TWIN project targets first gas as early as 2028, and the wider European LNG terminal and pipeline buildout is sized against import-capacity growth running through 2030. Not scored above 85 because the acute price spike itself, the part retail will actually notice, most plausibly resolves or fades within this single heating season rather than persisting for the full length of the window. Repair note: the original Bloomberg URL for the 18-year-low fact returns 403 to every fetch tool available this session, and this session's tools cannot retrieve Wayback Machine snapshots at all (a categorical block, confirmed on this URL and several others), so it could not be confirmed directly. It has been replaced with a Yahoo Finance syndication of the same Bloomberg wire story, fetched and confirmed directly. Separately: the candidate card that seeded this appraisal, CAND-20260829-05, headlines this same storage fact as a '13-year low' (sourced to Guardian World, 2026-08-29), while the business-press coverage this appraisal could fetch and verify calls it an 18-year seasonal low, dated 2026-08-03. No fetchable copy of the Guardian piece was found this session, so the two figures were not reconciled; this appraisal scores off the figure it could verify and flags the discrepancy for whoever chains this occurrence next rather than silently picking one.

LEAKY is not a recommendation to drop this candidate. The money is real (a confirmed EU LNG run rate of roughly 54 billion euros a year plus a further 84.1 billion euros of committed import-capacity buildout, with pipeline gas, the larger half by volume, adding more that no fetchable source this session could put an exact current-year euro figure on), and the candidate's own named chain, LNG import infrastructure, floating storage, and non-Russian pipeline suppliers, already points at the listed half of the split found here: Equinor, Shell, TotalEnergies on the supply side, and National Grid, Enagas and similar regulated terminal operators on the infrastructure side. What this appraisal adds is that the other half of the money, Sonatrach, SOCAR, QatarEnergy and the remaining sanctioned Russian volumes, is not reachable and should not be implicitly priced into a chain build's headline sizing. A chain build here should start from the non-Russian supply and infrastructure layer rather than from the EU-wide storage or price numbers themselves.
